title: Fast and slow pointers
sub: Linked List Cycle, the cycle entry with a proof, and Remove Nth Node From End: one pass and O(1) memory
cards/0/title: A cycle in a list: the problem and the naive solution
cards/0/body:
Linked List Cycle (LeetCode #141). Given the head of a list, does it contain a cycle — a node from which following next brings you back to it? Up to 10⁴ nodes. On LeetCode the cycle is described by a number pos — the index of the node the tail links to (−1 means no cycle), but it is not passed to the function. The follow-up: O(1) memory.

Naively: remember visited nodes in a HashSet<ListNode>. Meet a node a second time — there is a cycle; reach null — there is not. O(n) time and O(n) memory. The comparison here is by reference: ListNode does not override Equals and GetHashCode, so the set tells objects apart, not val values — two nodes holding the same number stay different.

More generally: any sequence x → f(x) over a finite set eventually loops — a path of “a tail, then a ring”, shaped like the letter ρ. A list is a special case: f(node) = node.next. That is why the same technique works for numbers too: the “happy number” (#202, repeat “sum of squares of the digits”) and finding a repeat in an array (#287, jumps i → nums[i]).
cards/1/title: Floyd’s idea: the tortoise and the hare
cards/1/body:
Two pointers start at the head: slow moves one node at a time, fast moves two. With no cycle, fast hits null after n/2 steps. With a cycle, both end up in the ring sooner or later, and there fast gains on slow by one node per step.

Why it cannot jump over. Say that in the ring fast is d nodes behind slow. In one step slow moves 1 and fast moves 2: the gap becomes d − 1. It shrinks by exactly one and will reach zero — zero cannot be skipped. And d is less than the ring length λ, so they meet within λ steps after slow enters the ring. In total O(μ + λ) = O(n), where μ is the length of the tail before the ring. Memory O(1).

The condition fast != null && fast.next != null checks both links that fast jumps through: without the second check, on an odd-length list fast lands on the last node and fast.next.next throws NullReferenceException.

The same pair finds the middle of a list (Middle of the Linked List, #876): when fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the way.
cards/2/q: Where do fast and slow pointers apply? Select all.
cards/2/options/0: Find the middle of a list in one pass without counting its length
cards/2/options/1: Decide whether “replace the number with the sum of squares of its digits” reaches 1 or loops forever
cards/2/options/2: In an array of n + 1 numbers from 1 to n, find the repeated one without modifying the array and with O(1) memory
cards/2/options/3: Find the k-th largest element of an array
cards/2/options/4: Check that the brackets in a string are balanced
cards/2/explain: The middle: fast at the end means slow is in the middle. The sum of squares of digits is a sequence x → f(x) over a finite set: it either reaches 1 or loops (#202). An array of 1…n of length n + 1 is the same kind of sequence, i → nums[i], and the repeat is the entry of its cycle (#287). The k-th largest and the brackets are not about a sequence of jumps: they need a heap and a stack.
cards/3/task: Step through 8 nodes where the tail 7 links back to node 2. The rig stops twice and asks where the pointers move.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: slow → 4, fast → null: the list ended
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: slow is on node 3, fast on 6. The tail of the list is node 7, and it links to 2. Where do the pointers move?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: fast jumps over two links: 6 → 7 → 2. There is no node 8, and there will never be a null: the tail 7 links back to 2. Now fast is behind slow in the ring and starts catching up.
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: slow → 6, fast → 5: the gap stays the same
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: slow is on 5, fast on 4 — one node behind. What happens on the next step?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: slow: 5 → 6, fast: 4 → 5 → 6. The gap was 1 and shrank by exactly 1 — to zero. It cannot jump over: every step closes the gap by one, so it cannot pass zero.
cards/4/title: The cycle entry (#142) and the proof
cards/4/body:
Linked List Cycle II (LeetCode #142): return the node where the cycle begins, or null; the list must not be modified, memory O(1). Naively a HashSet finds the entry too: the first node met a second time is the entry. But that is O(n) memory.

Let μ be the number of steps from the head to the entry and λ the ring length. Say they meet after k steps: slow has followed k links, fast 2k. Both stand on the same ring node, so the difference 2k − k = k is a whole number of laps: k is divisible by λ.

Now the key part. From the meeting point take μ more steps — that makes k + μ from the head. The first μ of them led to the entry, the remaining k are whole laps that bring you back to the same place. So μ steps after the meeting point you are at the entry. And μ steps from the head is the entry too. Put one pointer at the head, leave the other at the meeting point and move both one step at a time: they coincide exactly at the entry. You never need to know μ in advance.

On the trace: the tail 7 links to 2, so μ = 2 and λ = 6. They meet at node 6 after k = 6 steps — exactly one lap. From the head: 0 → 1 → 2; from the meeting point: 6 → 7 → 2. The entry is node 2. Time O(n), memory O(1).
cards/4/flow/0: phase 1: slow +1, fast +2 until they meet
cards/4/flow/1: k is a multiple of λ
cards/4/flow/2: p = head, slow stays at the meeting point
cards/5/q: From the head to the cycle entry is 3 steps (μ = 3), and the ring has 4 nodes (λ = 4). The pointers have met. Put p at the head, leave slow at the meeting point and move both one step at a time. Where and when do they coincide?
cards/5/options/0: After 3 steps, at the cycle entry
cards/5/options/1: After 4 steps, at the meeting point
cards/5/explain: Here they meet after k = 4 steps — exactly one lap. p gets from the head to the entry in μ = 3 steps. By then slow has made k + 3 steps from the head: 3 to the entry plus k = 4 more — a whole lap back to the entry. They coincide after μ = 3 steps, at the entry.
cards/5/wrong/1: After 3 steps both are already at the entry, and the phase 2 loop stops there. p never gets to the meeting point: the code returns the entry.
cards/5/wrong/2: The difference λ − μ means nothing. The key is that k is a multiple of λ, so from the meeting point to the entry is exactly μ steps (modulo whole laps).
cards/6/title: Remove Nth Node From End: a gap of n + 1
cards/6/body:
Remove Nth Node From End of List (LeetCode #19). Remove the n-th node from the end and return the head; 1–30 nodes, 1 ≤ n ≤ length. The follow-up: in one pass.

The naive way is two passes: count the length L, walk to the node before the (L − n + 1)-th and cut out the next one. That is O(L) and acceptable, but one pass is requested.

The idea — a fixed gap. fast runs n + 1 steps ahead, then both move together. When fast becomes null, slow is exactly n + 1 behind the end — that is, it stands before the node to delete, and slow.next = slow.next.next cuts it out. Why n + 1 and not n: to cut a node out of a singly linked list you need its predecessor.

Why a dummy. If n equals the length, the head itself must go, and it has no predecessor. A dummy node before the head always provides one: both pointers start at dummy, and the answer is dummy.next. Time O(L), memory O(1).
cards/7/q: Assemble the one-pass removal of the n-th node from the end.
cards/7/explain: fast runs n + 1 ahead: then slow stops before the target. Move while fast is not null. Cut it out: slow.next = slow.next.next (null would chop off the whole tail). Return dummy.next, not head: if the head was removed, head points to the node that was cut out.
cards/8/task: Step through 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with n = 5 — remove the fifth from the end, which is the head. The rig stops right before the cut.
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Nothing: slow never moved, there is nothing to remove
cards/8/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: NullReferenceException: the head has no predecessor
cards/8/goal/asks/0/q: fast has run n + 1 = 6 steps and is already null, while slow is still on D. What does the code do?
cards/8/goal/asks/0/explain: The while never ran, but slow is already where it needs to be: before the fifth from the end, that is, before the head. slow.next = slow.next.next cuts out 1, and the answer is dummy.next = 2. Without the dummy the head would have no predecessor, and you would need a separate case.
cards/9/q: A version without a dummy. On [1, 2] with n = 2 it crashes with a NullReferenceException. Tap the line where that happens.
cards/9/explain: After the for loop fast has passed both nodes and become null, and fast.next on null throws. This is exactly the “remove the head” case: n equals the length, and the target has no predecessor. The cure is a dummy node before the head (or a separate check if (fast == null) return head.next).
cards/10/title: Floyd beyond lists, and where it shows up in games
cards/10/body:
A repeat in an array (Find the Duplicate Number, #287): n + 1 numbers from 1 to n, do not modify the array, O(1) memory. Treat the array as a list: index i links to nums[i]. The repeated number is a node with two or more incoming arrows (the repeat may occur more than twice), and on a ρ-shaped path there is exactly one such node — the cycle entry. No arrow leads into index 0 (there are no zero values), so the tail starts there. The rest is exactly the two phases of #142.

In a game. Data linked by a “next” reference: a patrol route of waypoints, each with a next field; a chain of quests or dialogue lines. Is the route closed, and at which waypoint does the loop start — that is #141 and #142. In an editor tool a HashSet is simpler: memory is not tight, and the code is obvious. Floyd is needed when the “nodes” are not objects but values of a function with nowhere to store them: the period of a pseudo-random number generator, for example, is found exactly this way.

At an interview it pays to name both versions and what each costs: a HashSet takes O(n) memory and a hash on every step, Floyd takes O(1) memory but roughly three times as many link traversals.
cards/10/deep:
Why speeds 1 and 2. What matters is the difference in speed: it is 1, so the gap in the ring shrinks one at a time. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap shrinks by 2 per step: with an even λ and an odd initial gap the pointers never meet. Speed 2 is the slowest that still catches up, and the cheapest in link traversals.

The cycle length. After the meeting, keep one pointer in place and walk the other one step at a time until it comes back: the number of steps is λ. That is the follow-up “and how long is the cycle?”.

Brent’s algorithm. One pointer stands still, the other walks; after 1, 2, 4, 8 … steps the standing one is moved to where the walker is. The meeting gives λ directly, and μ is then found by a second pass with a gap of λ. It usually makes fewer link traversals (evaluations of f) than Floyd — that matters when f is expensive, like a generator step or a hash function. The complexity is the same: O(μ + λ) time, O(1) memory.

The cost of HashSet<ListNode>. The hash of a reference object without an overridden GetHashCode is RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode: it is assigned to the object on the first call and lives in its header or in an auxiliary runtime structure. For 10⁴ nodes that is nothing; but at an interview what matters is that you understand what is compared — the reference, not val.
cards/11/q: Which statements are true? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: fast at speed 2 cannot jump over slow in the ring: the gap shrinks by exactly 1 per step
cards/11/options/1: To find the cycle entry you first have to compute the tail length μ
cards/11/options/2: HashSet<ListNode> tells nodes apart by reference, even if they have the same val
cards/11/options/3: In #19, if n equals the list length, without a dummy you need a separate case for removing the head
cards/11/options/4: The condition while (fast.next != null) is enough for HasCycle
cards/11/explain: The gap shrinks one at a time and passes through zero — no jumping over. You do not need μ: two pointers, from the head and from the meeting point, converge at the entry after μ steps on their own. ListNode does not override Equals, so the set compares references. With n equal to the length the head is removed, and it has no predecessor — the dummy provides one. Without the fast != null check, after a jump fast.next.next = null the next check of fast.next throws NullReferenceException.
cards/12/q: You are solving Linked List Cycle II out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: return the entry node or null, do not modify the list, O(1) memory
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive approach: a HashSet of visited nodes — the first repeat is the entry, O(n) memory
cards/12/items/2: Phase 1: slow by 1, fast by 2; if they meet there is a cycle, if fast hits null there is not
cards/12/items/3: Prove it: the step count to the meeting, k, is a multiple of λ, so μ steps from the meeting lead to the entry
cards/12/items/4: Phase 2: one pointer at the head, the other at the meeting point, both one step at a time until they coincide
cards/12/items/5: Run the example: μ = 2, λ = 6, they meet at node 6, the entry is node 2
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O(n), memory O(1); edge cases: an empty list, a single node looping to itself
cards/12/explain: The problem and the baseline, then the two phases, with the proof between them: it explains why the second phase works. Then a run and the complexity. A node looping to itself: they meet on it, and p == slow right away — the entry is found with no steps.

cards/13/pairs/0/1: slow by 1, fast by 2: a meeting means a cycle
cards/13/pairs/1/1: The head and the meeting point, both one step at a time
cards/13/pairs/2/0: The middle of a list in one pass
cards/13/pairs/2/1: fast at the end — slow in the middle
cards/13/pairs/3/0: The n-th node from the end in one pass
cards/13/pairs/3/1: A gap of n + 1 from a dummy
